newsitem.title: USA: Mich. gaming board sets Detroit casinos timeline.
newsitem.headline: Mich. gaming board sets Detroit casinos timeline.

text.p: Michigan gaming officials and Detroit Mayor Dennis Archer have released plans for finding a site for casinos in the city within two months and a timeline for awarding licenses for them as soon as early 1998.
Michigan voters last November narrowly approved a referendum to allow three casinos in Detroit that backers have said could generate more than $100 million annually in tax revenue.

During a meeting of Michigan Gaming Control Board Tuesday night, representatives of the mayor's task force for casino development and the gaming board unveiled timelines for implementing the referendum.

Archer plans to release the task force findings June 13, which would include a proposed location for the casinos, appropriate size for them and the scope of what they could offer, press secretary Anthony Neely said.

Shortly thereafter, Archer plans to issue a request for proposal and then pare the applicants to six finalists by Aug 8. Three potential licensees would be chosen by Nov 10 and further negotiations would proceed, under Archer's planned timeline.
The state gaming board, now in the middle of drafting rules, could be ready to accept applications and begin investigating them by Sept 1, interim executive director Nelson Westrin said.

Under the gaming board timeline, a casino license could be issued as early as Jan 31, 1998. Applicants to the state board must first have completed a casino development agreement with Detroit, Westrin noted.
Westrin said as many as 20 companies have expressed interest in developing a casino in Detroit. He called the work of the board and the city task force a cooperative effort.
Gov. John Engler had opposed the casino referendum, but has appointed a bi-partisan board to oversee their development, Westrin said.
Archer wants the process nearly complete by the end of the year and construction to begin in early 1998, Neely said.
"It's the first time we have nailed down specific days, actually set deadlines to follow and made sure of every step of the process," Neely said.

The mayor, and other backers of the casino referendum, believe that about $1 million of gambling business leaves Michigan for Windsor, Ontario, every day, Neely said. Most of that business comes from Detroit and the mayor wants to capture it, he said.
The Lac Vieux Desert Band of the Lake Superior Chippewa Indians recently filed a federal lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Michigan challenging the state-wide casino referendum.

The lawsuit filed in February challenges licensing preferences within the referendum. It also contends that the tribes have exclusive rights to operate electronic games of chance in Michigan under both a federal court order and an agreement with the state.
Both Neely and Westrin said that the claims of exclusivity would not hold water.
The gaming control board has submitted proposed legislation to eliminate those preferences, which were "greatly overstated," Westrin said.
